title: Showcase: the adder magic trick
summary: The family sets A and B, they call the answer before the display shows it, then reveal why the trick cannot miss.
materials: the week 3 adder, still wired: micro:bit, edge connector and breadboard with both buttons

steps.title: Rehearse like a magician
steps.body:
Today the adder stops being a project and becomes a show. The design loop still runs it: ask, imagine, plan. Ask: what could go wrong live? Imagine each way the show could stumble: a loose wire, a tired battery, a case you never tried. Plan the rehearsal that catches every one of them before the audience sits down.

A breadboard that sat untouched for a few days deserves suspicion. Check every wire against your week 3 notes, reseat anything that wiggles, and run the program once to see the display wake up.

Then rehearse the whole trick alone. There are exactly four shows the buttons can put on: both off, only A on, only B on, both on. Press all four, and each time say the answer out loud before the display shows it: what the sum shows, what the carry shows. A magician never performs a trick that was not tested that same day.

Set the stage: adder in the middle of the table, whiteboard nearby but face down. The table on the whiteboard is the reveal, so nobody sees it early.

Five minutes on your typing site before the show. Warm up on the home row, then type the sprint's own words one last time: def, and, or, xor, import. Every one of them is wired into the trick on the table, and warm fingers make for a steady demo.

steps.title: Why four checks settle it forever
steps.body:
Here is a strange and wonderful thing about your adder: you can be completely certain about it, not just pretty sure.

Most claims about the world cannot be checked case by case. Nobody can test every apple to prove that all apples fall. But your adder has exactly two inputs, and each one is either on or off. Two choices for A and two for B make 2 x 2, which is 4 possible worlds, and that is all the worlds there are. Press all four and you have not sampled what the adder does, you have seen every single thing it will ever be asked to do. That is why the trick cannot miss: it is a test-it claim, and you tested all of it.

Now feel how fast that luxury disappears. An adder for two 8-light numbers has 16 inputs, and 16 on-off choices make 2 to the power 16 worlds, more than sixty five thousand presses. Real chips add numbers with 64 lights. Nobody presses every case there. Instead, engineers build big adders out of small pieces they have fully checked, the way yours chains one sum answer and one carry answer. Certainty at the bottom, stacked into towers.

figure.alt: The showcase table with the adder in the middle and the whiteboard, face down, off to one side, family members gathered around and a camera pointed at the scene. A note explains a volunteer sets the buttons and the builder calls the sum and carry before the display shows them, then the whiteboard flips over for the reveal.

items.s: Volunteer sets buttons; builder calls sum and carry
Reveal: flip whiteboard, match table rows to the presses

steps.title: Run the show
steps.body:
Gather the family. One volunteer sets the buttons any way they like. Before the display settles, you call it: what the sum shows, what the carry shows. Then everyone looks.

Run at least six rounds and let them try to trip you. They will discover something on their own: there are only four different settings, so by round five they are repeating themselves, and you can say so with a grin.

Then flip the whiteboard and give the reveal. Draw the table with four rows: A off B off, A on B off, A off B on, A on B on. Fill in sum and carry for each row, and connect each row to a press the family just watched. Say the two secrets out loud: the sum answers the question do A and B disagree, and the carry answers the question are both on. Four rows, four presses, no fifth case for a mistake to hide in. That is why it cannot miss.
checklist: I tested all four cases alone before anyone watched
I called every answer before the display showed it
The reveal matched each table row to a press the family saw
Somebody tried to trip the adder and could not

steps.title: Two fresh ideas for the gift page
steps.body:
The free build idea page opened in week 1, and a showcase never ends without feeding it. Week 8 will name the person the gift is for, so the page needs real choices to pick from.

While the family is still gathered, ask each person: what small machine would make your week better? Listen for problems, not products: cold tea, a plant nobody remembers to water, a door that slams.

Then add at least two fresh ideas to the page. Each idea gets one line with three parts: who it is for, the thing that bugs them, and a first guess at what the machine would do. No judging today, no prices, no picking. The page is a net, not a scale.
checklist: I asked every person in the room what would make their week better
At least two new ideas are on the page
Each idea names a person and the thing that bugs them
Nothing on the page got a yes or a no today

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: A video of one full round: the family sets the buttons, you call the answer, the display agrees. Catch the whiteboard reveal too if the camera can stay up for it.

extras.title: Rewrite your best log
extras.body:
Your logs are the writing you do here, and writing gets better by rewriting, not by more of it. Pick your best log from this sprint and rewrite it once.

1. Read the log out loud. Mark every sentence that tries to say two things.
2. Rewrite so each sentence carries one idea. Split, do not shorten.
3. Find every adjective (hard, cool, weird) and replace it with a number or a fact: how many tries, how long, what broke.
4. Put the reason before the claim: "the loop ran twice, so the heart flashed twice" rather than "the heart flashed twice, because the loop ran twice".
5. Read both versions to someone and ask which one they could follow without you in the room.

What to notice: the rewrite is usually shorter and says more. That is the whole trick.
